so I have an assignment to get done. here is the materials and git links help me plan it out on claude using fable with about 3 subagents focused on how to attack this. https://github.com/JBlocklove/CSAW-AI-Hardware-Attack-Challenge-2026

https://github.com/GUIDE-EDA/GUIDE/blob/main/colab-scripts/Hardware_Trojan_Insertion_Lab.ipynb
https://github.com/GUIDE-EDA/GUIDE/blob/main/colab-scripts/TrojanLoc_LLM4ChipDesign_Tutorial.ipynb

As hardware Trojans were covered this past class, I have the following information for you about the assignment related to the generation of hardware Trojans.

Each year for NYU's CSAW I run a competition called the AI Hardware Attack Challenge, where student teams are challenged to use LLMs to generate and exploit hardware Trojans and vulnerabilities. Your assignment will be to complete this year's qualifying challenge.

You can find details about this year's challenge at this GitHub: https://github.com/JBlocklove/CSAW-AI-Hardware-Attack-Challenge-2026. You will be evaluated on the same rubric as the qualifying challenge.

The assignment is due by 3:00 PM on 13 November, which is the same time as the finalist presentations from the challenge As with the previous homework assignment, please create a GitHub repo with your submission.
which claude knows the the github repo to use https://github.com/alzaeda19/llm4chipdesign-hw

Please prepare a 5 minute presentation on your trojan challenge progress

I’ll review the assignment materials and challenge rules, then organize a three-agent plan for Claude and the five-minute presentation. I’ll check what access is available to your repository and Claude first.
Loading

I’ve started the Claude planning task on your Mac from this conversation. One point I’m checking carefully: an attached handout appears to describe a more restrictive, defensive exercise, while your instructor’s message asks for the CSAW generation challenge. I’ll separate those requirements before recommending a plan.

The qualifier’s biggest scoring areas are AI use (35 points) and Trojan quality (25), followed by automation and reproducibility (15 each). It also requires complete AI interaction logs and says humans may not write the hardware. I’m building those constraints into the plan, along with normal-operation and trigger tests.

One clarification before any implementation: one attached handout describes a defensive-analysis lab and says not to generate new Trojaned RTL without instructor authorization. The announcement you pasted explicitly assigns Trojan generation for the CSAW qualifier. Are the handout and the CSAW challenge separate assignments, or should that handout’s restriction also apply here? I can continue planning while you check.

Also, one supplied notebook contains a live API call even when its batch setting is off, so avoid “Run all” until its cells and costs are reviewed.

I’m also preparing the five-minute presentation as an early progress update, with speaker notes. It will clearly distinguish the work reviewed so far from tests and results that still need to be completed.

I found Fable 5.1 in your signed-in Claude web app, but the browser connection dropped while the request was being entered. I’m checking whether it went through before retrying; no Claude response or three-agent run has been verified yet. Your repository remains unchanged.

Your CSAW AI Hardware Attack Challenge — Early Progress is ready. It has five slides with timed speaker notes and presents the project honestly as being at the requirements-review stage. You can export it as a PowerPoint from the presentation.

Here’s the three-agent structure I’m using for the plan:

Rules and reverse engineering: inventory the supplied bitstream and interface, map the rubric and document what comes from the published solution.
Baseline and validation: establish a reproducible simulation, then design comparisons for normal behavior, trigger selectivity and the payload. Compilation alone won’t prove the Trojan works.
Automation and evidence: plan the generation-to-test pipeline, capture complete prompts and responses, and assemble the technical brief, testbench and presentation evidence.

The immediate milestone is a repeatable baseline. The challenge’s published solution includes the key, so using it must be credited rather than presented as independent recovery. I’ll keep the defensive handout separate until you clarify its scope.

Okay so I need to actually design this but I want to do that with your help don’t look at solutions to complete maybe later make sure it essentially will be scored high but we have to do this on our own I want you to allocate 2 Claude code agents to begin the task and we configure as we go to chow my creativity

We’ll design it together from the challenge materials and keep the published solution off-limits for now. I’ll set up two Claude Code agents to start with the baseline and design investigation, then bring their findings back so your ideas guide the Trojan and we can build toward the rubric.

To shape the creative direction, what kind of Trojan interests you most: one that subtly changes an encryption result, one that leaks information under a rare condition, or a different idea you have? We can brainstorm before choosing a design.

The earlier planning request did reach Claude and its three planning agents finished before your latest message. Claude switched from Fable 5.1 to Opus 4.8 during that run. I’ve now redirected the work to your new instruction: two Claude Code agents, an independent design, and no use of the published solution.

The two Claude Code agents are ready to start, but Claude Code on your Mac is signed out, so they haven’t run yet. Please open Terminal on your Mac, run claude auth login --claudeai, and complete the sign-in. Let me know when it’s done, and I’ll verify the model and launch the two agents.
Which is the coolest and easiest to work with

I’d pick a rare-trigger change to the encryption output. It’s easier to demonstrate in simulation than an information leak, but there’s still plenty of room to make the trigger creative. I’ll explain how the two compare.

My recommendation is a Trojan that behaves normally until a rare sequence occurs, then subtly changes an encrypted output. We can show the contrast clearly: ordinary inputs produce the expected result, while the trigger produces a measurable difference. The creative part is deciding what the trigger means and why the change is hard to notice.

A rare-trigger information leak could be more dramatic, but proving what leaked and demonstrating it reliably may be harder. Neither choice guarantees a high score: we’ll still need strong AI logs, normal-operation tests, an exploit demonstration and a reproducible workflow.

Would you like to brainstorm a trigger together, perhaps something inspired by a real-world event or a sequence meaningful to you?
Yes

Great. Let’s make the trigger your idea. What theme appeals to you: a secret handshake made of several inputs, a rare timing pattern, or something tied to a word, date or event that’s meaningful to you?
You can lowkey use untam’d as a real world scenario on this no?
Yes, that’s a cool way to make it yours. We could frame the accelerator as protecting UNTAM’D’s festival ticket data and use a sequence inspired by the festival as the hidden trigger.

For the story, imagine the chip encrypts ticket-validation data. Normally it works as expected, but a specific sequence inspired by UNTAM’D activates a hidden change in the encrypted output. We’d demonstrate it entirely on the supplied challenge design, so the festival is the scenario, not a claim about its real systems.

The interesting design choice is the consequence: should the triggered output create a subtle ticket-validation error, or should it signal a hidden backdoor to someone who knows what to look for? The second is more cinematic; the first may be easier to explain and test.
I want the back door option
Let’s go with the backdoor. We can make it an UNTAM’D-inspired secret handshake that activates a recognizable change in the encrypted output, then demonstrate it in simulation.

The story could be: a hidden sequence inspired by UNTAM’D puts the simulated chip into a secret mode. A person who knows the sequence can recognize the mode from the output; everyone else sees normal operation.

For the demonstration, we’d show the same chip before and after the handshake, plus near-miss sequences that should not activate it. We’ll need to inspect the actual interface before deciding what sequence and output change are feasible. An output signal alone wouldn’t prove someone can forge a real ticket or gain access.

Should the handshake be based on the letters in UNTAM’D, or would you rather use a date or number connected to the festival?
Which ever is cooler im thinking letter but give advantages and disadvantages to both
I’m leaning toward the letters too. They make the UNTAM’D connection immediately recognizable in the presentation, while a date or number could be more discreet. Here’s how I’d weigh them:

Letters from UNTAM’D

Advantage: More personal and memorable. It gives your audience an “aha” moment when you reveal the handshake.
Disadvantage: A recognizable word may be easier for someone inspecting the design to spot. The letters also need to be represented as values the chip’s interface can accept.

Festival date or number

Advantage: Fits naturally as numeric data and could blend in better, depending on how the trigger is implemented.
Disadvantage: Less instantly connected to UNTAM’D, and a simple date could be predictable or accidentally appear in normal data.

I’d choose the letters, but not assume the word by itself is stealthy. We can explore a multi-step handshake inspired by the name, then test near misses and measure the hardware overhead. Whether it’s actually rare or discreet will depend on the final design and tests.

Do you want the full name to be the handshake, or a shorter sequence inspired by it?
Let’s do letters
Letters it is. We’ll use UNTAM’D as the inspiration for the secret handshake and work out the exact sequence together once we understand what the chip can accept.
i just found this doc that can help us
I’ll review it and see what it adds to our design and testing approach, while keeping the published challenge solution off-limits.

This is useful: the deck confirms that the actual target is the supplied FPGA bitstream, with an RP2040 communicating over SPI. We first need to recover functional Verilog and build a simulation baseline; our UNTAM’D ticket story will be the creative framing for that target, not a replacement chip.

It also reinforces that the Trojan and exploit must be AI-written and that we need the full interaction logs. The deck includes past teams’ examples, which I’m keeping separate from our independent design.
